result:
Solution 1 is most likely correct.

**Checking the small cases.** The 6×6 table in Solutions 1 and 2 is valid. Each row is the full divisor set of its r_i, and the table is symmetric, so the columns also work. So S(3) = 6, and Solution 3's value of 9 is wrong. S(2) = 2 is also fine.

**Why n = 10 fails (so S(5) ≠ 10).** The number r_i appears in some column j, so r_i divides c_j. Since c_j also has n divisors, c_j = r_i. Hence every r_i is some c_j, and the columns are the same numbers as the rows.

For n = 10, each r_i is q⁴·r or q⁹.
- Take r_i = q⁴·r. The divisor q³·r of r_i must lie in a column k with q³·r dividing c_k. The only 10-divisor numbers that q³·r divides are q⁴·r itself, so k = i. But that cell already holds r_i, so the divisor q³·r has no free column.
- For r_i = q⁹, the divisor q⁸ gives the same contradiction.

So n = 10 is impossible. By the same argument, any n whose smaller multiples of p fail needs the ordered-pair construction. That is consistent with Solution 1's S(p) = p(p−1) for p = 5, 7, 11, 13, which gives 20, 42, 110, 156. I did not independently check that p(p−1) is the minimum for p ≥ 7, so that part rests on the pattern.

The sum is 2 + 6 + 20 + 42 + 110 + 156 = 336. Solution 2's 10, 14, 22, 26 are ruled out at least for p = 5 by the argument above.

CHOICE: 1
